tweets.text:
what are some mega funding rounds that actually worked?

hardly any coming to mind.

there are so many horrible examples of projects that raised hundreds of millions and have barely delivered anything in years, or are even already dead.

meanwhile, many of the biggest success stories never had access to big funding. Hyperliquid took no private funding at all. Collector Crypt raised less than a million in private rounds. PumpFun printed half a billion on a 2M pre-seed.

funding is obviously a necessary evil. but in crypto, where you don't need massive resources for hardware or scaling, it tells you nothing about the likelihood of future success.

only founder-market fit and obsession do.

a very expensive lesson for a lot of early stage investors, IF they ever learn it.

THE DAILY METALS PULSE | Friday, November 27  
Asia Close / Europe Morning  
#Uranium #Silver #Gold #Copper

🥈 Silver futures jump 10% as the metals rally reaches London

New York silver futures traded at $44.22 an ounce during the European morning, up 10.4%. Gold futures gained 4.1% to $3,681.90, and platinum rose 8.8% to $1,351.50. European mining shares joined the rally, gaining 3.5% in early trading against 0.9% for the STOXX 600.

🏭 Copper hits $12,400 as Chinese industrial profits accelerate

Shanghai copper climbed as much as 5.2%, its biggest intraday gain since January. By 09:48 CET, three-month copper in London was up 4.6% at $12,400.50 a tonne, on course for its first weekly gain in seven weeks.

China’s industrial profits rose 20.1% year on year in October, up from 14.4% in September. Profits at China’s nonferrous metal miners rose 60.2% in the first ten months of the year as demand from the AI and new-energy sectors helped lift base-metal prices.

📊 Inflation expectations rise in the euro area

The ECB’s October survey showed that households expect prices to rise 3.5% over the next year, up from 3.1% in September. For gold, I’m watching whether US Treasury yields and the dollar rise together when New York opens. That would test how much of this morning’s rebound bullion can hold.

👀 What I’m watching this afternoon

• 14:30 CET · 8:30 a.m. ET — US goods trade and inventory figures are due. I’ll be watching the dollar’s reaction.

• 15:30 CET · 9:30 a.m. ET — Wall Street reopens after Thanksgiving. Can silver hold $44, and will North American copper and uranium miners follow Europe higher?

• 19:00 CET · 1 p.m. ET — The NYSE closes early. The next Platts uranium spot assessment is due Monday, so today I’m watching how uranium equities trade into the close.

the best signal you can look for right now if you want to maximize your returns next year:

what a team does while its token is down 80-90%.

9 out of 10 founders whine about the market and use it as the excuse for why things aren't working. not their fault, of course. some go quiet and wait for the market to come back so they can extract again. others just rug and move on to the next shiny thing.

but there's that rare 1 in 10 that only shows what it's really made of in a bear market. they're so obsessed that market conditions don't matter to them anyway. they see it as a chance to improve their fundamentals even further: less noise, full focus on the product, and market share to take while weaker competitors slowly bleed out.

those are the teams compounding their fundamentals right now, with pipelines stacked with big news. their comeback will be just as reflexive, while the rest stays dead.

I've watched this play out through three bear markets now. every time, it was both the best filter for finding these teams and the best time to load up on them.

stop crying and go find the 1 in 10.

If you bought $10,000 of Bitcoin at the October 2025 top, it's worth about $4,900 today.

• The good news is we're in the same zone where the last 3 bottoms formed.
• The bad news is there might be one more 13% drop first.

Here are the 5 signals I'm watching:

1. Coins in profit: bullish

On November 20, only about 43% of all Bitcoin was worth more than what people paid for it.

That's lower than right after the 2022 bottom.

This number has been under 45% on about 150 days in Bitcoin's history. A year later, BTC was higher every time.

2. Realized price: bearish

Realized price is about what the average holder paid for their BTC. Right now that's about $53.3K, and BTC is around $61.2K.

At the last 3 bottoms, BTC fell to that price or lower before it turned around. It hasn't done that yet.

So my two favorite signals disagree, and honestly I don't know which one wins this time.

3. Long-term holders selling at a loss: bearish for now

On November 20, people who held for a long time sold their coins for about 36% less than they paid.

This kind of selling can go on for weeks. I want to see the losses get smaller while the price holds.

4. ETF flows: bearish

For me this is the big one.

People have pulled about $5.4B out of US Bitcoin ETFs so far in November. That's already the worst month since these funds launched.

Def a leading indicator to pay attention to.

5. Miners: just starting to hurt

The average miner is losing money right now. Earlier this year it cost them about $75K to make 1 BTC, and BTC is around $61.2K.

The total power miners use is down about 7% from a year ago, and a signal called the Hash Ribbon just flipped. It flips when miners start shutting off machines.

The last time it flipped was late November 2025. It took about 3 months for miners to bounce back, and at past bottoms, that bounce back was the real buy signal.

There's a twist this time though. A lot of big miners are moving their power to AI data centers because it pays more.

Some of these machines are getting shut off for a better business, so I trust this signal a bit less than before.

So, is the bottom in?

I think this is a good area to start buying slowly. I just wouldn't call it the bottom yet.

Buying a little now and keeping some cash works either way. If this is the bottom, you're in. If it drops more, you can buy more.

Before I'd buy bigger, I want to see:

• BTC holding $55K to $60K
• Long-term holders selling at smaller losses
• Money coming back into the ETFs
• Miners starting to recover

Do you think Bitcoin has already bottomed, or is there one more drop coming?

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
The most insightful analogy I've read on the Jensen Huang story comes from a WeChat post that recently spread like wildfire in Chinese tech circles - before being deleted.

They called the whole saga 清君侧 (qīng jūn cè): "clearing the ruler’s side."

It means absolutely nothing to anyone outside China, but any fluent Chinese speaker with knowledge of Chinese history knows immediately what this refers to.

It has always been, throughout Chinese history and ever since the Han dynasty, the primary pretext for rebellion. 

You are not rising against the emperor - of course not, you would never do that! You are merely ridding him of the "evil" advisors around him who have led him astray.

The most famous early use of this expression in Chinese history is during the so-called Rebellion of the Seven States in 154 BCE, when 7 regional kings rose against the Han emperor under the slogan "execute Chao Cuo, clear the ruler’s side" (诛晁错，清君侧 - zhū Cháo Cuò, qīng jūn cè).

Chao Cuo was the emperor's top adviser and the architect of a policy to rein in these powerful regional leaders. Openly rebelling against the emperor would have made these leaders traitors, so they claimed to be targeting only his "evil" adviser. 

The emperor - to his discredit - gave in and had Chao Cuo executed, hoping it would end the revolt. It predictably didn’t work: freed from their main opposition inside the imperial palace, the rebels pressed their advantage and marched on the capital, and were only ultimately crushed at the cost of a full-blown civil war.

Rings a bell?

If you followed the Jensen Huang story, it's eerily similar to what happened. With American characteristics, of course.

In the role of Chao Cuo: Jensen Huang, who had successfully advised Trump - this story's "emperor" - to change policy with regards to AI and allow Nvidia to sell more powerful chips to China, as well as to keep open the loophole that enabled Chinese companies to rent Nvidia's advanced chips in data centers across Southeast Asia.

In the role of our rebellious regional kings, the China hawks around Trump, who of course would never dream of going against the president - they were merely protecting him from someone at his side supposedly compromised by a "Chinese spy".

Our "regional kings" are a broad coalition: hawks inside the administration like Marco Rubio (who wrote the memo that conveniently leaked - https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/11/13/behind-jensen-huangs-spy-scandal-shadow-war-trumps-ear-china/ - and that we now know contained false accusations - https://x.com/RnaudBertrand/status/2125761883055767910?s=20), Democrats like Elizabeth Warren who've been pushing bill after bill to tighten chip exports, media outlets like the New York Times, which printed the accusations without a shred of evidence, and, last but not least, Anthropic, the AI company at the origin of the export controls in the first place.

This is a bit of an aside but, in case you didn't know, as revealed in Kevin Roose’s new book "The AGI Chronicles" (in chapter 20 in case you want to check), the export controls that limit the sales of Nvidia chips to China were first drafted by Dario Amodei himself and his co-founder Jack Clark in Dario's backyard. They then sent it to Ben Buchanan who had been brought into the Biden administration to advise on tech-related issues: he loved it and the rest is history. Ben Buchanan, incidentally, became an adviser to Anthropic once he left government - nothing to see here...

Back to our "clear the ruler’s side" analogy.

Trump, for all the mockery he gets, showed a better grasp of statecraft here than a Han emperor: he refused to sacrifice his Chao Cuo.

By his own account, he personally convinced Nvidia's board to bring Huang back, 12 days after his ouster. Whatever one thinks of him, he understood what the Han emperor hadn't: the hawks are ultimately after power, and every "adviser" you let them take only makes them stronger.

In this instance, it's all somewhat moot though: the hawks may not have succeeded in taking Huang down but in a curious inversion of the Chao Cuo story, they won on policy instead. 

The rebels of 154 BCE got their minister's head, only to see the emperor rein in the regional kings anyway. The hawks of 2026 failed to get Huang's head, but got almost everything he had fought against: the remote-access loophole is closed, data centers across Southeast Asia now need licenses, and Nvidia itself, while Huang was out, announced it would no longer ship its licensed H200s to China (https://www.scmp.com/tech/article/3374812/nvidia-board-says-it-has-no-plans-reinstate-jensen-huang-ceo) and its latest outlook assumes no data center revenue from China at all (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1045810/000104581026000088/q3fy27cfocommentary.htm). 

In other words, ironically, while the pretext for the rebellion failed - they failed to "clear the ruler's side" - the rebellion itself seems to have succeeded, so far at least.

Maybe Trump isn't smarter than our Han emperor after all...

This is the topic of my latest article: a painstakingly well-sourced and detailed look at who really tried to push Jensen Huang out, and how a spy accusation nobody has ever substantiated managed to shift US policy on AI.

As I write in the article's conclusion, it's a story in which we all lost. 

We lost, first, on how this was decided. The fate of what had been the world's most valuable company, and of America's policy on the most consequential technology of our age, was shifted by a classified memo written in the shadows, built on an unfounded accusation, illegally leaked, and reported with complete disregard for any journalistic standard.

Due process, shareholder rights, the laws protecting classified information, the presumption of innocence, the basic duty of a newspaper to check what it prints: every formal rule that was supposed to stand in the way simply didn't.

If the thought of the technology that will shape humanity's future being decided like this doesn't send chills down your spine, you... need to read my article, I guess.

And that's before we even get to what was decided, which should worry you even more.

To read the full story, here's the link to my article: https://arnaudbertrand.substack.com/p/clearing-the-rulers-side-jensen-huang?r=4r0pw&utm_campaign=post&utm_medium=web&showWelcomeOnShare=true

crypto entropy - a drift towards chaos and instability.

your skills and experience in crypto peaks at like 2nd cycle and then (paradoxically) gradually decays over time. 

most accounts here become washed, some of them eventually pivot to scamming and/or become too unstable and mentally deranged. they end up posting some absurd bullshit. with time people stop paying attention and they just end up talking to a brick wall like a true schizo. I’m sure you know at least one or two accounts that used to be relevant but now just tweeting some absolute bullshit with abysmal engagement. Some of them love to block everyone they disagree with which results in them being in this solo echo chamber where they continue to lose their sanity. 

I call this entropy of crypto - the continuous tendency of a system to become increasingly chaotic and unstable.

crypto is a very weird place that does not reward you for your time here, instead it punishes you into making your experience irrelevant. learning curve peaks early and then you stuck with all the traumas and PTSD that will only mess with your head and impair your decision making. there are no trends in crypto - everything is one time only event and never comes back so there is no useful knowledge for you to use next time. I’ll give examples: 
NFTs? happened once and never really returned 
GameFi? SocialFi? happened once and never really returned
IDOs? happened once and never really returned. 
Your favourite L1 or L2 ecosystem? Remember AVAX eco in 2021? happened once and probably never comes back. 
…and list goes on. every cycle there is a meta and it never really comes back again. Crypto is a disposable industry. It’s always easier to rug the project which starts to lose relevance and launch a new one instead of trying to fix it. Or do a rebrand and launch new ticker to delete the old price chart. happened many times. 

you either die a hero or live long enough to see yourself become the scammer
